entry: Urban process in which more affluent residents and investment change a [[Neighbourhood|neighborhood]]'s character. There is no agreed definition, and the term is sometimes used pejoratively. Gentrification often increases economic value, but it can change a neighborhood's demographic makeup and displace incumbent residents. Critics allege forced displacement of minority and working-class residents, while some peer-reviewed studies find limited causal links to substantially elevated displacement. The British sociologist Ruth Glass first used the term in its current sense in 1964, describing middle-class people displacing working-class residents in [[London]].

Taxonomic rank above species and below family, used for living and fossil organisms and for viruses. The genus name forms the first part of each species' [[Binomial nomenclature|binomial name]]. For example, *Panthera leo* (lion) and *Panthera onca* (jaguar) are two species in the genus *Panthera*, which lies within the family [[Felidae]]. The word comes from Latin *genus*, cognate with *gignere* ("to bear; to give birth to"). Swedish taxonomist [[Carl Linnaeus]] popularized its use in his 1753 *Species Plantarum*.

Science of determining the age of rocks, fossils and sediments using signatures inherent in the rocks themselves. Absolute geochronology relies on radioactive isotopes, while relative geochronology uses tools such as paleomagnetism and stable isotope ratios. Combining several geochronological and biostratigraphic indicators improves the precision of an age. Biostratigraphy places rocks within an interval of time by their fossil assemblages but gives no direct absolute age. Radiometric methods measure the decay of a radioactive parent isotope with a known [[Half-life|half-life]] into its radiogenic product. Uranium–lead dating, often applied to the mineral [[Zircon]] in igneous rocks, is one of the two most commonly used methods for geologic dating, along with argon–argon dating. Uranium–thorium dating is used for [[Coral|corals]], speleothems, carbonates and fossil bones. Geochronology is the prime tool of chronostratigraphy, which seeks absolute ages for fossil assemblages and the geologic history of Earth.

Science of measuring and representing the geometry, gravity and spatial orientation of Earth in time-varying three-dimensional space. The word derives from [[Ancient Greek]] *geodaisia*, "division of Earth." Geodesy provides the scientific basis for mapping, navigation and positioning, and supports infrastructure development, natural resource management and mineral exploration. Its measurements underpin the geospatial reference frames used in transportation, satellite systems, global trade and timekeeping. Geodynamic studies cover crustal motion, tides and polar motion. The 1980 Geodetic Reference System (GRS 80), with a semi-major axis of 6,378,137 m and a flattening of 1:298.257, is the basis for [[Global Positioning System|GPS]] positioning. Geomatics, including [[Surveying|surveying]], applies geodesy at local and regional scales.

Reference frame for representing the position of locations on Earth. Datums are crucial to [[Geodesy|geodesy]], navigation, surveying, geographic information systems, remote sensing and cartography. A horizontal datum measures position across Earth's surface as latitude and longitude, and a vertical datum measures elevation or depth relative to a standard origin such as [[Sea level|mean sea level]]. A standard datum consists of a model of Earth's shape (a reference ellipsoid or [[Geoid|geoid]]), an origin tied to a monumented location, and control points measured from that origin. The relationship between coordinates in different datums is undefined and can only be approximated; the disparity between two datums can reach kilometers, a discrepancy called datum shift. Since the rise of the global positioning system, the WGS 84 datum has supplanted most others in many applications, although local datums such as OSGB36 approximate particular areas more closely.

Species of very large saltwater clam (*Panopea generosa*) in the family Hiatellidae. Native to the eastern North Pacific Ocean from [[Alaska]] to Baja California, it is the largest burrowing clam in the world. Its shell measures 15 cm to over 20 cm, but its siphons can extend to 1 m. The typical lifespan is about 140 years, and the oldest recorded individual was 179 years old; annual rings in the shell allow ages to be determined. The clam filters [[Plankton|plankton]] from water drawn through its siphon. Its common name derives from the Lushootseed name *gʷidəq*.

English poet and civil servant, best known for *The Canterbury Tales*. Called the "father of English literature," he was the first writer buried in what became Poets' Corner in [[Westminster Abbey]]. His father, John Chaucer, was a wine merchant with a royal appointment, and Chaucer became a page in the household of Elizabeth de Burgh, Countess of Ulster, in 1357. In 1359, early in the [[Hundred Years' War]], he served with the English army in France; in 1360 he was captured during the siege of Reims, and the king paid £16 for his ransom. He later worked as a courtier, diplomat and Clerk of the King's Works from 1389 to 1391. His works include *The Book of the Duchess*, *Troilus and Criseyde*, *The House of Fame* and *The Legend of Good Women*. His work helped legitimize [[Middle English]] as a literary language when French and Latin were still dominant. Almost 2,000 English words are first attested in Chaucerian manuscripts.

British-Canadian computer scientist and cognitive psychologist, known for his work on artificial [[Neural network (machine learning)|neural networks]] and called the "Godfather of AI." With David Rumelhart and Ronald J. Williams, he co-authored a 1986 paper that popularized the backpropagation algorithm for training multi-layer networks. AlexNet, designed with his students Alex Krizhevsky and Ilya Sutskever, won the ImageNet challenge in 2012. Hinton shared the 2018 Turing Award with Yoshua Bengio and Yann LeCun, and the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics with John Hopfield. He worked for [[Google]] from 2013 to 2023 and resigned in May 2023 to speak freely about the risks of AI, including misuse, technological unemployment and existential risk.

Australian actor. Known for often playing eccentric roles on stage and screen, Rush won the Academy Award for Best Actor for *Shine* (1996) and a Primetime Emmy Award for portraying Peter Sellers in the [[HBO]] film *The Life and Death of Peter Sellers* (2004). He also won the Tony Award for Best Actor in a Play for *Exit the King* (2009), making him the only Australian to achieve the Triple Crown of Acting. His film roles include Captain Hector Barbossa in the *Pirates of the Caribbean* franchise. He was named 2012 Australian of the Year. Born in Toowoomba, [[Queensland]], he trained in Paris at L'École Internationale de Théâtre Jacques Lecoq.

Spherical or geodetic system for measuring and communicating positions on Earth as latitude and longitude. It is the simplest, oldest and most widely used type of spatial reference system, and it forms the basis for most others. Its measurements are angles rather than Cartesian coordinates, and a full specification includes a [[Geodetic datum|geodetic datum]], since different datums yield different coordinates for the same location. The system is credited to [[Eratosthenes|Eratosthenes of Cyrene]], who composed his now-lost *Geography* at the [[Library of Alexandria]] in the 3rd century BC. [[Hipparchus]] determined latitude from stellar measurements and longitude from lunar eclipses. In his 2nd-century *Geography*, [[Ptolemy]] measured latitude from the [[Equator]]. At the International Meridian Conference of 1884, 22 of the 25 nations represented agreed to adopt the longitude of the Royal Observatory at Greenwich, England, as zero. France adopted [[Greenwich Mean Time]] in 1911.

Integrated computer hardware and software that store, manage, analyze, edit, output and visualize geographic data. A [[Database|spatial database]] is usual but not essential, and in a broader sense a GIS includes human users, procedures and institutions. GIS relates unrelated information through location as the "key index variable," with places recorded by longitude, latitude and elevation. It is used in engineering, [[Urban planning|planning]], transport, insurance, telecommunications and business, as well as in [[Forestry]], ecology and Earth science. Roger Tomlinson first coined the phrase in the mid-1960s, though many underlying methods are older. Early examples come from epidemiology: in 1832 the French cartographer Charles Picquet mapped cholera deaths across 48 districts of Paris, and in 1854 [[John Snow]] traced the source of a [[Cholera]] outbreak in London by plotting casualties' residences against water sources. GIScience, the academic study of these systems, is often considered a subdiscipline of [[Technical geography]].

Shape that Earth's ocean would take under gravity and rotation alone, without winds or tides. [[Carl Friedrich Gauss]], who first described it, called it the "mathematical figure of the Earth." The geoid results from the uneven distribution of mass within Earth and can be known only through extensive gravitational measurements. It was not defined precisely until satellite geodesy in the mid-20th century, when the mathematician Gladys West first synthesized a high-fidelity geoid from satellite data. The geoid is irregular but considerably smoother than Earth's surface, and its deviation from a reference ellipsoid ranges from +85 m (Iceland) to −106 m (southern India). It serves as a reference surface for heights and is an essential component of satellite-based systems such as the [[Global Positioning System]].

Standardized system relating rock strata to geologic time. It arranges the rock record in chronological order using chronostratigraphy, and uses [[Geochronology|geochronology]], such as radiometric dating, to date the boundaries between units. The scale covers about 4.54 ± 0.05 billion years of Earth history. International units are defined by the International Commission on Stratigraphy (ICS), a constituent body of the International Union of Geological Sciences. The [[Phanerozoic]] eon is split into the [[Paleozoic]], [[Mesozoic]] and [[Cenozoic]] eras, each subdivided into periods such as the [[Cretaceous]] and [[Quaternary]]. Boundaries are ratified through Global Boundary Stratotype Sections and Points (GSSPs), which are reference rock layers. The base of the Quaternary was adjusted to 2.58 million years in 2009 on climatic and glacial evidence.

Sequence of major geological events in Earth's past, dated by the [[Geologic time scale|geologic time scale]]. Earth formed about 4.54 billion years ago by accretion from the solar nebula, the disk of dust and gas left over from the formation of the [[Sun]]. Initially molten from volcanism and collisions, its outer layer cooled into a solid crust once water began accumulating in the atmosphere. The [[Moon]] may have formed after a protoplanet struck Earth. Outgassing and volcanism produced the primordial atmosphere, and condensing water vapor, augmented by ice from asteroids, produced the oceans. Continents formed, broke apart and recombined into [[Supercontinent|supercontinents]]. The earliest known, Rodinia, began to break apart about 750 million years ago; Pannotia formed 600 to 540 million years ago, and [[Pangaea]] broke apart 200 million years ago. The present pattern of [[Ice age|ice ages]] began about 40 million years ago, and the Last Glacial Period ended about 10,000 years ago.

Family of moths in the order [[Lepidoptera]], named for the looping gait of its caterpillars. The name derives from Greek *geo* ("earth") and *metron* ("measure"), because the larvae, called inchworms, loopers or spanworms, appear to measure the ground as they move. Many geometrid caterpillars have only two or three pairs of prolegs at the rear instead of the usual five. Many are green, grey or brown and hide by resembling twigs. Adults have slender abdomens and broad wings usually held flat, which makes them look [[Butterfly|butterfly]]-like, though they are typical moths; most fly at night. The family includes the peppered moth, *Biston betularia*, which has been widely studied in population genetics, and several notorious pests, among them the fall cankerworm and winter moth.

Discrete probability distribution for the number of independent trials needed to get a first success. It takes two forms: the number X of Bernoulli trials until one success, supported on 1, 2, 3, …, and the number Y = X − 1 of failures before the first success, supported on 0, 1, 2, …. If each trial succeeds with probability p, then P(X = k) = (1 − p)ᵏ⁻¹p. It is the only memoryless discrete distribution, the discrete counterpart of the [[Exponential distribution|exponential distribution]]. Rolling a six-sided die until a 1 appears gives a geometric distribution with p = 1/6. The distribution is sometimes called the Furry distribution after Wendell H. Furry.

Sum of the terms of a geometric progression, in which each term is the previous term multiplied by a constant common ratio *r*. The finite sum *a* + *ar* + … + *arⁿ* equals *a*(1 − *r*ⁿ⁺¹)/(1 − *r*) for *r* ≠ 1. For |*r*| < 1, the infinite series converges to *a*/(1 − *r*); for example, ½ + ¼ + ⅛ + … sums to 1. [[Zeno's paradoxes]] of the 5th century BCE have been interpreted as involving geometric series, which Greek mathematicians later studied formally. [[Archimedes]] used one to calculate the area inside a [[Parabola|parabola]] in the 3rd century BCE. Geometric series are used in mathematical finance, in calculating areas of fractals, and in computer science.

Scientific study of the origin and evolution of topographic and bathymetric features generated by physical, chemical or biological processes at or near Earth's surface. Geomorphologists explain why landscapes look as they do and predict change through field observations, physical experiments and numerical modeling. Surface processes include the action of water, wind, ice, wildfire and life, along with soil-forming reactions and gravity. Geologic processes such as mountain uplift, volcanic growth and the formation of sedimentary basins also shape landscapes, and climate and tectonics can feed back on each other. Subfields include [[Glacier|glacial]] geomorphology, which studies [[Moraine|moraines]] and other deposits, and fluvial geomorphology, which studies how rivers transport [[Sediment|sediment]] and cut bedrock. The field draws on [[Geology]], [[Geodesy]] and [[Climatology]].

Physical science concerned with the processes and properties of Earth and its surrounding space environment, studied by quantitative and observational methods. It focuses on Earth's shape, its gravitational, magnetic and electromagnetic fields, and its internal structure and dynamics, including [[Plate tectonics|tectonics]] and volcanism. The field also covers the oceans, atmosphere, [[Cryosphere]], ionosphere and magnetosphere, and analogous processes on the [[Moon]] and other planets. One of the oldest sciences, it dates to early seismometers and magnetic compasses and later to Newtonian analyses of [[Tide|tides]]. Methods include field measurements, laboratory experiments, remote sensing, numerical modeling and signal processing. Seismic waves recorded at several locations can locate earthquakes, which informs knowledge of plate tectonics and mantle convection. Applications include mineral and energy exploration, natural hazard mitigation and groundwater studies.

German mathematician who helped create [[Set theory|set theory]], now a fundamental theory in mathematics. He established the importance of one-to-one correspondence between sets, defined infinite and well-ordered sets, and proved that the [[Real number|real numbers]] are more numerous than the [[Natural number|natural numbers]]. His method implies an infinity of infinities, and he defined cardinal and ordinal numbers and their arithmetic. His theory of transfinite numbers met resistance from contemporaries including Leopold Kronecker, [[Henri Poincaré]] and [[Ludwig Wittgenstein]]. [[David Hilbert]] defended the work against its critics. The Royal Society awarded Cantor its Sylvester Medal in 1904. A devout Lutheran, Cantor believed the theory had been communicated to him by God. His recurring depression from 1884 has been blamed on hostile reception, and some have attributed it to bipolar disorder.

German mathematician and physicist. As a school teacher, Ohm began research with the new electrochemical cell invented by Italian scientist [[Alessandro Volta]]. Using equipment of his own creation, he found that the potential difference (voltage) applied across a conductor is directly proportional to the resulting electric current, a relation known as [[Ohm's law]]. He published this in *Die galvanische Kette, mathematisch bearbeitet* (1827), but the work initially met resistance, partly because of its emphasis on mathematical modeling over empirical description. He taught at the Jesuit Gymnasium of [[Cologne]] from 1817, and in 1852 was appointed to the chair of physics at the University of [[Munich]]. The Royal Society awarded him the Copley Medal in 1841. The unit of electrical resistance, the [[Ohm]], was adopted internationally in 1881.

German philosopher and a major figure of German idealism. Born in [[Stuttgart]], Hegel lived through the transition from the Enlightenment to Romanticism, and his thought was shaped by the [[French Revolution]] and the [[Napoleonic Wars]]. His principal achievement was a comprehensive system of absolute idealism in which reality is a unified whole, centered on *Geist* ("spirit"), humankind coming to know itself through rational historical development. His [[Dialectic|dialectical]] method reveals the contradictions in concepts and resolves them in a higher unity that both cancels and preserves the earlier stage. The *Phenomenology of Spirit* (1807) and *Science of Logic* (1812–1816) set out this system. He held the chair of philosophy at the University of Berlin. After his death his followers split into Right and Left Hegelian camps; the Left, including [[Karl Marx]], adapted his method for materialist critiques of religion and society. His thought became a major reference point for [[Existentialism]].

United States cavalry commander. Custer graduated last in his class at the [[United States Military Academy|West Point]] in 1861, as the [[American Civil War]] began. He rose to brevet general during the war, commanding the Michigan Brigade at the [[Battle of Gettysburg]] and defeating Confederate cavalry under J. E. B. Stuart. After the war he led the 7th Cavalry Regiment in campaigns against Plains tribes. He was killed at the [[Battle of the Little Bighorn]] along with every soldier of the five companies he led, an event known as "Custer's Last Stand." Assessments of his judgment there remain divided, with some blaming tactical overreach and others intelligence failures.

Ballet choreographer of Georgian descent. Born in [[Saint Petersburg|Saint Petersburg]], Balanchine trained at the Imperial Ballet School and fused classical technique with styles he encountered on Broadway and in Hollywood to create his "neoclassical style." Invited to the [[United States]] in 1933 by arts patron Lincoln Kirstein, he co-founded the School of American Ballet in 1934 and the New York City Ballet in 1948, remaining its artistic director for more than 35 years. His works are often plotless ballets with minimal costume and décor, set to classical and neoclassical music. He worked closely with [[Igor Stravinsky]] and created more than 465 ballets, including *Agon* (1957) and *Jewels* (1967), the first full-length plotless ballet. He is styled the father of American ballet.

Anglo-Irish philosopher and bishop. Berkeley is regarded as the founder of immaterialism, which holds that material substance does not exist and that familiar objects are ideas perceived by minds. In *A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge* (1710) and *Three Dialogues Between Hylas and Philonous* (1713), he set out this view, with Hylas representing his opponents, in particular [[John Locke]]. He argued against [[Isaac Newton]]'s doctrine of absolute space, time and motion, and in *The Analyst* (1734) criticized the foundations of [[Calculus]]. His ideas influenced [[David Hume]] and [[Immanuel Kant]]. He served as Bishop of Cloyne from 1734 and pursued a failed plan for a missionary college in [[Bermuda]]. The city of Berkeley and [[University of California, Berkeley|the University of California, Berkeley]] are named after him.
